1.title: Cloud Native Architecture and Principles
1.text: Welcome to Module 12: Cloud Native Architecture and Principles. This module is in the Cloud Native Architecture domain, and it covers the topic called Cloud Native Architecture and Principles. By the end you will be able to do four things. State the C N C F cloud native definition and its example technologies. Compare a monolith with microservices, and recognize twelve-factor and resilience ideas. Describe serverless, event-driven design and open standards. And match the personas: developer, platform engineer, S R E, DevOps, security and FinOps.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Rethinks Its Design
1.text: The Harbor Books shop began as one program. It is now split into storefront, catalog, orders and more. The team wants each part to fail and recover alone, and the order confirmation job to run only when needed. A platform team offers self-service tools, and a site reliability engineer, an S R E, watches production. In this module you learn the vocabulary behind these choices.

1.title: The CNCF Cloud Native Definition
1.text: This slide is tagged moving. The C N C F definition says cloud native practices let organizations build and run workloads in public, private and hybrid clouds, at scale, in a repeatable way. Its marks are loosely coupled systems that interoperate, and that are secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable and observable. Typical examples are serverless, declarative A P Is, containers, microservices, service meshes, multi-tenancy and immutable infrastructure. The list is non-exhaustive. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, the current definition is version one point one, approved in February, twenty twenty-four. Exam tip: loosely coupled, plus the five qualities.

1.title: Monolith versus Microservices
1.text: A monolith holds all functionality in one deployable program. It is the simplest place to start, but it gets harder to maintain as it grows, and as more developers share the codebase. Microservices are independent services, each focused on one function, that appear to the user as one application. They can change and be released faster. The price is more parts to network, observe and secure, as in Module 6, Module 8 and Module 13. The diagram shows one large box, beside four small services. Exam tip: a monolith is one program, and microservices are many small services.

1.title: Twelve-Factor Ideas and Resilience
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Four ideas come from the twelve-factor manifesto. Keep config in the environment, outside the code. Run the app as stateless processes. Make processes disposable: they start and stop at a moment's notice, with fast startup and graceful shutdown. And treat logs as event streams. Three resilience settings matter too. A timeout is how long to wait for a reply, so a call succeeds or fails in a predictable time. A retry tries again a limited number of times. And a circuit breaker stops calling a failing service once a limit is reached. A service mesh can add these without code changes. Exam tip: retries heal blips, and a circuit breaker stops hammering a failing service.

1.title: Serverless, Functions and Event-Driven Design
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. With serverless, servers are abstracted away from you. You pay per use, and scaling is automatic. Knative Serving and OpenFaaS run serverless-style functions and containers on Kubernetes, and OpenFaaS can scale to zero. Event-driven design means components react to events, which are changes of state. CloudEvents describes event data in a common format, for interoperability. In the diagram, an order event triggers a function, which runs and then scales back down. Autoscaling links back to Module 5. Exam tip: serverless means no servers to manage, and event-driven means reacting to changes.

1.title: Open Standards and Portability
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. Four open standards surround Kubernetes. O C I defines the image format, runtime and distribution of containers. C R I defines how the kube let talks to a container runtime, for example containerd or C R I O. C N I defines how network plugins connect Pods, and C S I defines how storage drivers plug in. Because the interfaces are open, you can swap an implementation, and keep workloads portable across hybrid and multi-cloud setups. Exam tip: O C I for images, C R I for runtimes, C N I for networks, and C S I for storage.

1.title: Personas and Platform Engineering
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. Six personas to know. A developer writes the application and ships it along the delivery path. A platform engineer builds self-service tools and workflows that developers use. An S R E applies software engineering to operations, so that code running in production works. In DevOps, teams own the whole path from development to production operations. Security, or DevSecOps, adds security responsibilities to that path, as in Module 8. And FinOps is shared financial accountability for technology spend between engineering, finance and business. Backstage, hosted by the C N C F, is a framework for a developer portal. Exam tip: platform engineers build self-service tools, and S R Es keep production reliable.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Cloud Native Architecture
1.text: Six pairs to keep apart. The definition: loosely coupled systems that are secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable and observable, and the technology list is non-exhaustive. Monolith or microservices: one deployable program, or independent services. Serverless or event-driven: no servers to manage and automatic scaling, or reacting to events. O C I, C R I, C N I or C S I: images, runtimes, networks or storage. S R E, DevOps or platform engineering: reliability in production, shared ownership, or self-service tools. And immutable infrastructure: replace rather than change, with containers as the example. Exam tip: match the term to the problem it solves.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap. The definition is loosely coupled systems that are secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable and observable. For design, compare monolith with microservices, and know the twelve-factor ideas, and timeouts, retries and circuit breakers. Serverless means pay per use and automatic scaling, and CloudEvents describes events. The standards O C I, C R I, C N I and C S I keep parts swappable and workloads portable. And the personas are developer, platform engineer, S R E, DevOps, security and FinOps. Now five practice questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. According to the C N C F definition, which properties characterize cloud native systems? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The definition describes loosely coupled systems that are secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable and observable. It names public, private and hybrid clouds, and does not require any one language or license.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which statement compares a monolith with microservices correctly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A monolith holds all functionality in a single deployable program. Microservices break an application into independent services, each focused on a specific function, which can be changed and released faster.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Harbor Books wants an order confirmation function that runs only when an order event arrives, and scales down to zero otherwise. Which fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Serverless platforms run functions on demand, scale automatically and can scale to zero, so nothing runs between orders. The other objects keep a fixed set of Pods running all the time.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which standard defines how the kube let talks to a container runtime? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The Container Runtime Interface is how the kube let talks to a runtime such as containerd or C R I O. C N I is for networking, C S I for storage, and CloudEvents for event data.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which role builds self-service tools and workflows so that developers can ship software faster? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Platform engineering builds tools and processes, like a self-service station, that empower developers. S R Es focus on production reliability, FinOps on cost accountability, and DevSecOps on security.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, C: loosely coupled, secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable, observable. Question two, A: a monolith is one program, and microservices are independent services. Question three, D: a serverless platform runs functions on events and scales to zero. Question four, B: C R I connects the kube let and the runtime. Question five, C: platform engineers build self-service tools.
